buddhist-compassion: Karuna, usually translated as compassion, is the wish that all sentient beings be free from suffering, and it stands as one of the central virtues cultivated on the Buddhist path. It arises in response to the pervasive fact of dukkha, or unsatisfactoriness, that the Buddha identified at the heart of ordinary existence, and it is meant to be extended without limit to every being rather than reserved for kin or allies. In the Mahayana tradition especially, karuna is paired with wisdom and embodied in the bodhisattva, who vows to work for the liberation of others. Cultivated through meditation and ethical practice, it is understood not as mere sentiment but as an active, disciplined orientation of the mind.
nagarjuna-emptiness: Emptiness, or sunyata, is the teaching that all things lack any fixed, independent essence and exist only in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designation. It was developed most rigorously by the Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, who used relentless dialectical arguments to show that positing self-existent entities leads to contradiction. Rather than a claim that nothing exists, emptiness holds that things are real precisely because they are dependently arisen and thus without inherent nature. For Nagarjuna this insight dissolves the grasping and metaphysical confusion that bind beings to suffering.
zen: Zen is a school of Mahayana Buddhism, known as Chan in China and Zen in Japan, that emphasizes direct insight into one's own nature over reliance on scripture or doctrinal analysis. Growing from the meeting of Indian Buddhism with Chinese Daoist sensibilities, it stresses seated meditation, disciplined everyday practice, and transmission from teacher to student outside of written texts. Certain lineages employ the koan, a paradoxical question or story designed to exhaust discursive thinking and provoke a sudden shift in understanding. The aim throughout is awakening to reality as it is, unmediated by conceptual overlay.
atman-brahman: Atman and Brahman are the twin poles of much of classical Indian metaphysics: atman is the innermost self or consciousness, while Brahman is the ultimate, unconditioned ground of all reality. In the Advaita Vedanta system articulated by Shankara, the deepest teaching of the Upanishads is that these two are not different but identical, so that the true self is nothing other than the absolute. Ordinary experience of a separate, individual self is traced to ignorance, and liberation comes through the direct realization of this underlying unity. The position is a rigorous nondualism, holding that plurality and separateness are ultimately appearance rather than final truth.
dharma: Dharma is a foundational term across Indian thought whose meaning shifts with context, generally denoting the order, duty, law, or teaching that sustains both the cosmos and right human conduct. In Hindu ethics it names the moral and social obligations proper to one's station and circumstances, the righteous path that upholds a well-ordered life. In Buddhism the Dharma is the Buddha's teaching and, more broadly, the truth about the nature of things that the teaching points to. Common to these senses is the idea of a normative structure that living in accordance with brings harmony, and departing from brings disorder.
ahimsa: Ahimsa is the principle of nonviolence or non-harm toward all living beings, deeply rooted in the Jain, Hindu, and Buddhist traditions of India. It calls not only for the avoidance of physical injury but for restraint in thought and speech, resting on a sense of the kinship and value of all life. In the twentieth century Mahatma Gandhi made ahimsa the ethical and political core of his campaigns, fusing it with satyagraha, or the disciplined pursuit of truth, to resist injustice without inflicting harm. In his hands the ancient ideal became a practical method of collective, nonviolent action.
augustine-city-of-god: The doctrine of the two cities is Augustine of Hippo's account of human history as the intertwined story of two communities defined by what they love. The earthly city is formed by love of self carried to the point of contempt for God, while the heavenly city is formed by love of God carried to the point of contempt for self. Written partly to answer the charge that Christianity had caused Rome's fall, the framework distinguishes eternal spiritual allegiance from any particular political order. The two cities remain mingled in this world and are separated only at the final judgment.
augustine-time: Augustine's reflections on time, set out in his Confessions, confront the puzzle that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the present has no duration, so it becomes unclear how time can be real or measured at all. His influential proposal is that time is bound up with the mind's activity: we measure it as a kind of extension or distension of the soul, holding the past through memory, the present through attention, and the future through expectation. On this view time is not an independent container but is tied to the created order and to conscious experience. The discussion remains a touchstone for later philosophy of time and mind.
augustine-will: The divided will is Augustine of Hippo's analysis of the experience of wanting and not wanting the same thing, in which a person genuinely commands the will to act yet finds it resisting itself. Drawing on his own struggles, he argues that this internal conflict reveals not two natures but a single will fractured and weakened, unable to fully follow what it knows to be good. This condition he traces to the disordering effects of sin, from which the will cannot free itself by its own effort but requires divine grace. His treatment reshaped Western thinking about freedom, motivation, and the limits of self-mastery.
wheel-of-fortune: The wheel of fortune is the image, given lasting form by Boethius, of Fortune as a capricious goddess turning a wheel that raises some to prosperity while casting others down. It expresses the ancient insight that worldly goods such as wealth, power, and reputation are fickle and never truly in our possession. Boethius uses the figure to argue that because these gifts belong to Fortune's changeable nature, staking one's happiness on them guarantees eventual grief. The remedy he proposes is to seek a stable good beyond Fortune's reach. The motif went on to pervade medieval and Renaissance art and literature.
boethius-consolation: The Consolation of Philosophy is a work written by Boethius while awaiting execution, in which the personified figure of Philosophy visits the imprisoned author to heal his despair through reasoned dialogue. Alternating prose and verse, it argues that true happiness lies not in the transient gifts of Fortune but in the highest good, which is identified with God, and it confronts the problems of evil, providence, and the compatibility of divine foreknowledge with human freedom. Boethius resolves the last of these by distinguishing God's timeless, eternal vision from temporal necessity. Blending classical philosophy with a broadly theistic outlook, the book became one of the most widely read texts of the Middle Ages.
ontological-argument: The ontological argument, first formulated by Anselm of Canterbury, attempts to prove God's existence from the concept of God alone, without appeal to observation of the world. Anselm defines God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived and reasons that such a being must exist in reality and not merely in the mind, since a being that existed in reality would be greater. Uniquely among the classic proofs it is entirely a priori, moving from an idea to a conclusion about existence. It has provoked continuous debate, from Gaunilo's early objection through Kant's charge that existence is not a genuine predicate, and continues to attract both defenders and critics.
aquinas-natural-law: Natural law, as systematized by Thomas Aquinas, is the theory that there is an objective moral order accessible to human reason and grounded in the rational nature that all persons share. Aquinas holds that natural law is the rational creature's participation in the eternal law by which God governs creation, and that its first precept is to do good and avoid evil, from which more specific duties follow by reflecting on natural human goods such as life, knowledge, and society. Because it rests on reason rather than revelation, it is meant to bind all people regardless of faith or culture. The theory has profoundly shaped Western ethics, jurisprudence, and ideas of human rights.
aquinas-five-ways: The Five Ways are Thomas Aquinas's five concise arguments for the existence of God, presented at the opening of his Summa Theologiae. Each begins from a familiar feature of the observable world and reasons toward a necessary first cause: motion requires an unmoved mover, causation a first cause, contingency a necessary being, degrees of perfection a supreme measure, and the order of nature an intelligent designer. Aquinas identifies the terminus of each argument with what people call God. Drawing heavily on Aristotle, the Five Ways became a standard framework for natural theology and remain a focus of philosophical discussion.
aquinas-double-effect: The doctrine of double effect, whose classic formulation derives from Thomas Aquinas, addresses when it is permissible to perform an action that has both a good and a seriously harmful consequence. It holds that such an act may be justified if the act itself is not wrong, the good effect is what one intends while the harm is merely foreseen and not the means to the good, and the good achieved is proportionate to the harm allowed. Aquinas developed it in discussing self-defense, where preserving one's life is intended and the attacker's death is not. The principle remains central to debates in medical ethics, warfare, and moral philosophy about the difference between intending and merely foreseeing harm.
